Imagine a new, strange fruit arrives, and you don't know what it is. You check the three fruits in your basket that look most similar in size and color. If two are mangoes and one is a peach, you might decide your new fruit is a mango. This is exactly how k-Nearest Neighbours works!

Machine learning models help us classify things. One idea, k-Nearest Neighbours, decides by looking at its closest friends and taking a majority vote. Another, Decision Trees, plays a game of 'twenty questions', asking smart questions to sort things into clear groups. Both are powerful tools.

Let's try k-NN. Imagine points on a map. A new point arrives, and we want to classify it. If we look at just one neighbour, its class might be positive. But looking at three neighbours, it's still positive. Yet, with five neighbours, the answer actually changes to negative!

For exams, remember: k-NN needs features scaled, but decision trees don't. A 1-nearest neighbour model usually has zero training error, but it likely overfits, meaning it's memorized the data too much. Pruning helps trees avoid this. Always aim for a balanced model!
